title: Fund-Market Turmoil Hits Turkish Stocks as Pusula Collapse Spurs $1B Outflows
subhead: Ankara and the central bank stepped in to calm markets after a liquidity crunch triggered by the collapse of Pusula Portföy sent stocks sliding as much as 7.7% and investors pulled about $1 billion from funds. The episode tests Turkey's market credibility a year before a contested election cycle.

sections.heading: Markets: Fund-Run Stress After Pusula Collapse
sections.body:
Turkish equities suffered their sharpest stress in months as the collapse of asset manager Pusula Portföy triggered a broader liquidity crunch in the money-market and fund sector. Bloomberg reported that Turkish stocks fell more than 5% as fund redemption woes deepened, while Greek outlet Bankingnews put the intraday drop at up to 7.7% and said some $7.5 billion in fund assets were hit. The Financial Times framed the move as a 'fund run,' reporting that investors withdrew about $1 billion from Turkish funds.

According to Reuters and Bloomberg, authorities responded with emergency measures — liquidating stressed funds, imposing trading bans, and signaling central-bank support. Market Screener reported that the Turkish central bank moved to boost repo funding and ease liquidity conditions during the volatility. The turmoil traces back to Pusula, whose funds collapsed by around 90% and whose chairman was reported arrested, per IntelliNews and Startup Fortune; the episode also ensnared other names such as Tera and prompted questions about a Golden Global Bank money-market fund missing a payment (Newsquawk).
sections.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest test of Turkish market stability since the post-election disinflation drive, and it exposes lingering fragilities in a fund sector that boomed under high nominal returns. How Ankara manages the fallout will shape investor confidence and the lira well before the 2028 political calendar sharpens.

sections.heading: Foreign Policy: Ankara Pitches a Black Sea Shipping Truce
sections.body:
Turkey has proposed a Russia-Ukraine deal to halt attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, according to a source cited by Kyiv Post, Al Arabiya, Turkish Minute and Malay Mail. The plan reportedly revives a safe-passage mechanism for commercial vessels along the grain corridor, with Turkey offering to act as guarantor — a return to the role it played under the 2022 grain initiative.

The proposal comes amid an escalating naval drone campaign in the Black Sea: Reuters reported ships are adopting makeshift anti-drone defenses as attacks intensify, and The Kyiv Independent noted Ankara earlier summoned Ukraine's ambassador over strikes on ships in the region. The new initiative, floated from Ankara, positions Turkey as an indispensable intermediary in a conflict where it has tried to keep channels open to both Moscow and Kyiv.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is seeking to convert its position as the Black Sea's dominant littoral power into a diplomatic asset, reviving the grain-deal playbook to protect shipping and bolster its leverage with both capitals — while Washington is distracted by the US-Iran standoff in the Gulf.

sections.heading: Domestic Politics: Erdoğan's 2028 Term-Limit Push Gains Steam
sections.body:
Signals that Recep Tayyip Erdoğan will seek another term in 2028 strengthened this week. An adviser was reported by Algemeiner saying Erdoğan plans to seek reelection and circumvent constitutional term limits, while BGNES detailed a route by which a parliamentary vote could unlock five more years for a president already in his third decade of rule. Turkish Minute separately reported senior AKP figures floating early elections to enable another candidacy.

The mechanism under discussion would require a constitutional interpretation or parliamentary action to reset term counts — a move opposition parties and the Soufan Center's analysis warn would cement 'one-man rule' at a moment of institutional strain. The debate is gaining urgency as the AKP angles for a political calendar that could shield Erdoğan from the fallout of the current market stress.
sections.whyItMatters: A credible push for another Erdoğan term reframes the entire pre-election period: it raises the stakes for opposition consolidation, complicates any succession debate inside the AKP, and signals that Ankara's political trajectory — and its engagement with the West — is unlikely to be reset in the near term.

sections.heading: Syria & the Region: Fidan Puts Israel at Center of Stability Debate
sections.body:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking from Damascus, called Israel 'the greatest potential threat' to Syria's stability, according to Anadolu Agency and Yeni Safak. The remarks came as Ankara prepares for a landmark Erdoğan visit to Syria that The Economist notes has Israel worried, with Jerusalem Post analysis reading the trip as evidence of deepening Turkey-Damascus ties that could shift the balance of influence in the country.

Fidan also said the Mecca Alliance is advancing amid Houthi tensions (Türkiye Today), and condemned attacks on Saudi oil facilities (Hürriyet Daily News). Ankara simultaneously escalated rhetoric toward Athens over Greece's alliance with Israel, with Daily Sabah reporting Turkey warned Greece against partnering with a 'destabilizer' — an echo of the broader regional realignment as Turkey expands its Damascus footprint while Israel pushes back on Iranian and Turkish inroads.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is consolidating its position as the dominant external actor in post-Assad Syria, framing that role as a foil to Israeli influence in the Levant. The coming Erdoğan visit will likely lock in defense and trade arrangements that reshape the region's power map — and sharpen Ankara's confrontation with Israel's regional posture.

sections.heading: Energy: $108B Bet on Renewables Alongside Hydrocarbons
sections.body:
A new analysis (OilPrice) finds Turkey is betting $108 billion on wind and solar capacity while simultaneously expanding its oil and gas footprint — a dual-track strategy that reflects the government's push for energy independence. A Climate Action Tracker assessment of Türkiye's power sector describes the transformation as 'at a crossroads,' noting the tension between ambitious renewables growth and continued hydrocarbon investment.

The figures sit alongside Ankara's nuclear program, where Akkuyu is nearing commissioning and the government has signaled a wider nuclear cooperation with Russia, as reported in this brief yesterday. Turkey is effectively running three parallel tracks — Russian-backed nuclear, renewables buildout, and domestic gas — in a bid to reduce reliance on imported energy and hedge against volatile global prices.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is trying to have it both ways: scaling renewables to cut import dependence while deepening nuclear ties with Moscow and developing domestic gas. The balance Turkey strikes between these tracks will define its energy security, its leverage with Russia, and the credibility of its green-transition pledges to the EU.

bottomLine: Today's core story is financial, not geopolitical: the collapse of Pusula Portföy has triggered Turkey's worst fund-market stress in months, forcing the central bank and regulators into emergency liquidity and trading measures and prompting roughly $1 billion in outflows. That instability lands at a moment when Ankara is simultaneously pushing a new Erdoğan term, courting Damascus with a landmark visit, and relaunching its Black Sea mediator role via a civilian-shipping truce proposal to Russia and Ukraine. Turkey's near-term agenda is ambitious, but the market shock is the variable with the most immediate consequences — how the state manages this liquidity scare will set the tone for the lira, foreign investment, and the political calendar heading into 2027's electoral maneuvering.
sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, Financial Times, Bankingnews.gr, IntelliNews, Startup Fortune, Market Screener, Newsquawk, Kyiv Post, Al Arabiya, Turkish Minute, Malay Mail, Firstpost, Kyiv Independent, Anadolu Agency, Yeni Safak, Türkiye Today, Hürriyet Daily News, Daily Sabah, eKathimerini, The Economist, Jerusalem Post, New Arab, Enab Baladi, OilPrice.com, Climate Action Tracker, Algemeiner, BGNES, The Soufan Center
